what: A stream processor like Flink reads an endless flow of events (often from Kafka), groups and counts them as they arrive, and keeps running totals safe across crashes.
like: Like a scoreboard operator who updates the score after every play, instead of recounting the whole match at the end.
why: Fresh answers in seconds, not after tonight's batch job
Counts by when things really happened (event time), even if data arrives out of order
Checkpoints let it crash and resume without double counting

steps.d: The Kafka source reads crawler hits from each partition and remembers its offsets (its place in each partition), so it can rewind after a failure.
Each hit carries the time it happened (event time), not the time Flink saw it (processing time). Watermarks say 'event time has reached t', so windows know when to close.
keyBy(page) sends every hit for a page to the same task. A 1-minute tumbling window counts hits per page per minute; sliding and session windows are other shapes.
Running counts live in keyed state (RocksDB, or ForSt in Flink 2.0). Hits arriving after the watermark passed are late: allow some lateness, or send them to a side output.
Barriers flow through the job; each operator snapshots state. The Kafka sink pre-commits a transaction and commits only when the checkpoint completes, so results are written once.
If the sink slows down, buffers fill and Flink slows the source instead of dropping data. Checkpoint barriers slow too, which is why unaligned checkpoints exist.

numbers.l: classic window shapes: tumbling, sliding and session
Flink release (Dec 2017) that added two-phase commit sinks
first Kafka version with transactions, needed for exactly-once
Flink release that first added unaligned checkpoints
shorter checkpoints with Flink 2.0 disaggregated state, per VLDB paper

choices.d: How long to wait for out-of-order events before closing a window. Longer means more complete counts but slower results; shorter means fresher but more late data.
Tumbling for clean per-minute buckets, sliding for moving averages (say 5 minutes every 1 minute), session for bursts split by a gap of inactivity.
Drop it, allow lateness so windows update again, or route it to a side output that a batch job folds in later.
Shorter means less replay after a crash, but more overhead. With exactly-once Kafka sinks, readers see results only after each checkpoint, so it also sets output latency.
Heap state is fastest for small state. RocksDB spills to local disk for large state; Flink 2.0 ForSt keeps state in remote storage like S3.

instead.why: Hourly or nightly batch is simpler when minutes of delay are fine
Ingest raw events and aggregate at query time with materialized views
Kafka Streams library runs inside your app, no separate cluster
A simple INCR counter per page-minute when exactness is not needed

breaks.d: One idle Kafka partition sends no events, so the minimum watermark never moves and windows never close.
breaks.see: Output stops while input keeps flowing; current watermark metric flat
breaks.fix: Mark idle sources (withIdleness) so they do not hold back the watermark

breaks.d: Crawler logs arrive minutes late from some regions, after windows closed.
breaks.see: numLateRecordsDropped climbing; counts lower than the batch total
breaks.fix: Raise watermark delay or allowed lateness, or reconcile with a side output

breaks.d: A slow sink or a hot key makes upstream tasks wait.
breaks.see: Busy or backpressured tasks in the web UI; Kafka consumer lag growing
breaks.fix: Scale the slow operator, pre-aggregate hot keys, batch sink writes

breaks.d: Under backpressure, barriers queue behind data and checkpoints take too long.
breaks.see: Checkpoint duration rising, failed checkpoints in the UI
breaks.fix: Unaligned checkpoints, buffer debloating, fix the root backpressure

breaks.d: Keys for old pages or sessions are never cleared.
breaks.see: State size and checkpoint size grow every day
breaks.fix: State TTL, windows that close, RocksDB or ForSt for large state

say: Crawler hits land in Kafka; a Flink job keys by page and counts hits in 1-minute tumbling windows using event time from the log line.
I'll set a watermark a little behind the newest event to absorb out-of-order logs, and send anything later to a side output that we reconcile.
Checkpoints to S3 plus a transactional Kafka sink give exactly-once results, so a crash replays from the last checkpoint without double counting.
If one page is extremely hot, I pre-aggregate before the keyBy so a single task is not the bottleneck.

followups.q: Event time or processing time - when does it matter?
followups.a: Processing time is simpler and fastest, but replays and delays shift counts into the wrong minute. Event time gives the same answer every run, which matters for billing and reports.

followups.q: How does exactly-once work end to end?
followups.a: Flink checkpoints source offsets and state together. The Kafka sink writes inside a transaction that it pre-commits at the checkpoint and commits once the checkpoint completes. Downstream consumers read only committed data.

followups.q: How would you count unique pages crawled per bot per day?
followups.a: Key by bot, 1-day tumbling window, and a HyperLogLog sketch in state instead of a full set, so memory stays small for a close estimate.

followups.q: Flink or just ClickHouse materialized views?
followups.a: For simple counts, ClickHouse views are less to run. Flink earns its place with event-time windows, joins between streams, late-data rules and exactly-once outputs to other systems.

today: Flink 2.0 moves state to remote storage (disaggregated state with the ForSt store); its VLDB 2025 paper reports up to 94% shorter checkpoints and much faster recovery and rescaling than Flink 1.20.

check.q: A crawler log line is stamped 10:00:05 but reaches Flink at 10:03. Which time should a per-minute report use?
check.why: Event time puts the hit in the minute it really happened, so reruns give the same counts.

check.q: What does a watermark of 10:01 tell a window operator?
check.a: Event time has reached 10:01, so earlier windows can close
d: The job is 1 minute behind Kafka
check.why: Watermarks are Flink's event-time clock; windows ending at or before it can fire.

check.q: You want counts that reset every minute with no overlap. Which window?
check.why: Tumbling windows are fixed and non-overlapping. Sliding windows overlap, sessions close after a gap.

check.q: Why can checkpoints slow down when the job is backpressured?
check.a: Barriers wait in the same queues as the data
check.why: Aligned barriers travel with the records, so slow data means slow barriers. Unaligned checkpoints help.
